newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK tanker nears disputed islands.
newsitem.headline: HK tanker nears disputed islands.

text.p: A Hong Kong protest ship on Wednesday steamed towards disputed East China Sea islands which activists plan to reclaim from Japan, but the protest group said it would avoid a violent showdown with Japanese forces.
The rusty tanker Kien Hwa 2, carrying 18 Hong Kong activists, was set to arrive at the islands late at night (about 1430 GMT), Hong Kong government radio quoted correspondents on board as saying.

The activists vowed to reclaim the islands -- known to Chinese as the Diaoyus and to Japanese as the Senkakus -- by removing a Japanese-built lighthouse and raising a People's Republic of China red flag, the radio said.
But the group's spokesman in Hong Kong said they would not try to force their way on to the islands if they faced a strong Japanese military presence.
"Based on our principle of peaceful, rational, non-violent protest, and our members' safety, we will not make unnecessary sacrifices," Lew Mon-hung told reporters.
The wife of leading Diaoyu islands activist David Chan, who is on board the tanker, appealed to the Japanese government not to use force.

"I appeal to the Japanese government not to do any barbaric act that will endanger the lives of those on board the ship," Hing Chan said. She also said China ought to show more concern for the protesters and protect the vessel.
The tanker set sail from Hong Kong on Sunday and held to its course despite bad weather and mounting tension in the region over the dispute.

The islands have been the focus of anti-Japanese protests by Chinese communities across East Asia and in North America since a Japanese rightist group in July built the lighthouse and a war memorial on the islands to bolster Tokyo's sovereignty claim.
Hong Kong, a British colony with a predominantly Chinese population, reverts to Beijing rule next year.

On Monday, five vessels carrying about 20 protesters from Taiwan and Hong Kong and up to 60 journalists tried to reach the islands to tear down the lighthouse. They were repulsed by 17 Japanese patrol ships backed by a helicopter.
A Japanese coastguard spokesman said at least 13 Taiwan ships had tried and failed to get near the islands this month.
Hong Kong's chief civil servant, Anson Chan, fuelled the controversy in Hong Kong by referring to the islands by their Japanese name during a visit to Australia.

Shocked legislators in the colony called on Chan, the chief secretary, to explain herself. "I will demand an explanation from her in the coming session of the Legislative Council," said pro-China legislator Cheung Hon-chung.
China accuses Japan of occupying the islands and demands a withdrawal. In Hong Kong three quarters of a million people have signed petitions over the past month urging Japan to get out.
The Hong Kong activists who failed to land on the isles on Monday said they would make a second try next month.
"Our aim is to land on the Diaoyus and remove the lighthouse built by the Japanese youth group and other symbols, but we will proceed on a peaceful basis," group spokesman Au Pak-kuen said.

Japan has claimed sovereign rights to the islands and refused to acknowledge the dispute is open for discussion with China. Tokyo's sovereignty claim dates to 1895, when Japan defeated China and seized Taiwan and other territories. China has claimed sovereignty over the islands for centuries.
